**Monaco**,[[a]](#cite_note-10) officially the **Principality of Monaco**,[[b]](#cite_note-11) is a [sovereign](/wiki/Sovereign_state "Sovereign state") [city-state](/wiki/City-state "City-state") and [microstate](/wiki/European_microstates "European microstates") in [Western Europe](/wiki/Western_Europe "Western Europe"). Situated on the [French Riviera](/wiki/French_Riviera "French Riviera"), it is a [semi-enclave](/wiki/Enclave_and_exclave "Enclave and exclave") bordered by [France](/wiki/France "France") to the north, east, and west, with the [Mediterranean Sea](/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea "Mediterranean Sea") to the south; the [Italian region](/wiki/Regions_of_Italy "Regions of Italy") of [Liguria](/wiki/Liguria "Liguria") is about 15 km (9.3 mi) east.[[10]](#cite_note-12) With a population of 38,423 living in an area of 2.08 km2 (0.80 sq mi), Monaco is the [second smallest](/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_area "List of countries and dependencies by area") sovereign state in the world, after [Vatican City](/wiki/Vatican_City "Vatican City"), as well as the [most densely populated](/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population_density "List of countries and dependencies by population density"). It also has the world's shortest national coastline of any non-landlocked nation, at 3.83 km (2.38 mi).[[11]](#cite_note-13) Fewer than 10,000 of its residents are [Monégasque](/wiki/Mon%C3%A9gasque_people "Monégasque people") nationals.[[12]](#cite_note-14) Although [French](/wiki/French_language "French language") is the [official language](/wiki/Official_language "Official language") of Monaco, [Italian](/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language") and [Monégasque](/wiki/Mon%C3%A9gasque_dialect "Monégasque dialect") are also widely spoken and understood.[[c]](#cite_note-15)

The first major contribution of Woodward's career in the early 1940s was a series of papers describing the application of [ultraviolet](/wiki/Ultraviolet "Ultraviolet") [spectroscopy](/wiki/Spectroscopy "Spectroscopy") in the elucidation of the structure of natural products. Woodward collected together a large amount of empirical data, and then devised a series of rules later called the [Woodward's rules](/wiki/Woodward%27s_rules "Woodward's rules"), which could be applied to finding out the structures of new natural substances, as well as non-natural synthesized molecules. The expedient use of newly developed instrumental techniques was a characteristic Woodward exemplified throughout his career, and it marked a radical change from the extremely tedious and long chemical methods of structural elucidation that had been used until then.

In 1944, with his post doctoral researcher, [William von Eggers Doering](/wiki/William_von_Eggers_Doering "William von Eggers Doering"), Woodward reported the synthesis of the [alkaloid](/wiki/Alkaloid "Alkaloid") [quinine](/wiki/Quinine "Quinine"), used to treat [malaria](/wiki/Malaria "Malaria"). Although the synthesis was publicized as a breakthrough in procuring the hard to get medicinal compound from Japanese occupied southeast Asia, in reality it was too long and tedious to adopt on a practical scale. Nevertheless, it was a landmark for chemical synthesis. Woodward's particular insight in this synthesis was to realize that the German chemist Paul Rabe had converted a precursor of quinine called quinotoxine to quinine in 1905. Hence, a synthesis of quinotoxine (which Woodward actually synthesized) would establish a route to synthesizing quinine. When Woodward accomplished this feat, organic synthesis was still largely a matter of trial and error, and nobody thought that such complex structures could actually be constructed. From July 2004 through June 2008, he was the director of the Dartmouth Institute for Writing and Rhetoric.

In August 2024, prosecutors detained Ko to investigate a property development project from his time as mayor, and indicted him on bribery and other corruption charges in December 2024. Further information: [List of California wildfires](/wiki/List_of_California_wildfires "List of California wildfires")

The timing of "fire season" in California is variable, depending on the amount of prior winter and spring precipitation, the frequency and severity of weather such as heat waves and wind events, and moisture content in vegetation. [Northern California](/wiki/Northern_California "Northern California") typically sees wildfire activity between late spring and early fall, peaking in the summer with hotter and drier conditions. Occasional cold frontal passages can bring wind and lightning. The timing of fire season in Southern California is similar, peaking between late spring and fall. The severity and duration of peak activity in either part of the state is modulated in part by weather events: downslope/offshore wind events can lead to critical fire weather, while onshore flow and Pacific weather systems can bring conditions that hamper wildfire growth.[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-:02-12)
